title: Hash-Based Indexing
lead: A hash address tells us where to look, not which key we found. Follow collisions, overflow pages and a local split through one running example.
goals: Explain in-memory hashing and collision resolution
Trace searches, insertions, deletions, and overflow in static chained hashing
Recognise skew and identify when rehashing is needed
Simulate global and local depth, bucket splits, and directory changes in extendible hashing

sections.title: Choose a bucket, then compare the keys
sections.html:
Our ticket service needs to find ticket 10 quickly. Instead of keeping every code in order, divide each nonnegative code by four and use its remainder as an address: h(k)=k mod 4. This original example maps 6→2, 10→2 and 14→2. A bucket is the storage region at that address. The address narrows where to look, but finding bucket 2 has not established which of its keys is 10. Compare the stored keys to confirm equality. Distinct keys receiving the same address are a collision.

A range request exposes the limitation. To find all codes 6…14, bucket 2 alone misses 7,8,9,11,12,13 in other buckets. Numeric neighbours need not have neighbouring hash addresses. Hash indexes suit equality on a complete search key; ordered trees also support useful contiguous range scans. Equal-key grouping is useful beyond indexes, for duplicate elimination, GROUP BY and equijoins. The hash function organises candidates; the operator still enforces its semantics.

There are several ways to resolve collisions. In chaining, link additional entries or pages from their home bucket. In in-memory open addressing, search another slot by a consistent probe rule. Trace a tiny linear-probing example with four empty slots 0…3: insert 6 into 2; insert 10 into 3 because 2 is occupied; insert 14 into 0 after wrapping past 3. The array is [14,empty,6,10]. Finding 14 must probe 2,3,0 in that order. An empty slot introduced by naïve deletion can break a later lookup, so deletion needs a compatible policy. Disk buckets are page-based; this slot trace is a separate in-memory illustration.

Key takeaway

The same hash does not mean the same key. Hashing narrows down where to look; key comparisons are still needed to confirm a match.

sections.title: Follow overflow pages and count the actual reads
sections.html:
Keep four primary bucket pages and h(k)=k mod 4, now with room for two entries per page. Insert 6 then 10: bucket 2 is [6,10]. Inserting 14 cannot fit, so attach an overflow page [14]. Lookup 14 reads the primary page, compares 6 and 10, follows its link and finds 14. From a cold cache this is two page reads, despite computing h only once. This is static chained hashing: the number of primary buckets remains fixed.

h(14)=2
[6,10] → [14]

One uncached bucket with no overflow costs one read for lookup; changing it costs a read and a write, two I/Os before extra overhead. With a primary page and two overflow pages, an unsuccessful lookup needs all three reads. For a nonunique search key, finding the first match is insufficient: later pages can contain more. Delete 14 by locating its page, removing it and writing the changed page; an implementation may reclaim the empty overflow page. These counts concern bucket entries. If an entry stores a RID, returning a full row can require an additional table-page read. An on-disk directory can add reads too.

As the file grows, chains can grow unevenly; as it shrinks, primary pages can stay nearly empty. Rehashing to a new mapping can redistribute entries, but visits and rewrites the data. Static structure keeps bucket changes local, which can simplify concurrent updates, while a global rebuild is expensive. A fast hash computation is not enough if the mapping concentrates popular keys.

For example, k mod 16 uses the lowest four bits. Codes 0,16,32,48 all go to zero. Better mixing or another modulus may spread these distinct codes. It cannot split repeated copies of the same key under ordinary key-based hashing. A prime modulus is not proof against collisions. Database hash functions balance computation cost and distribution; linear hashing is another dynamic scheme, outside this lecture’s covered scope.

sections.title: Split one full bucket instead of rewriting them all
sections.html:
Could growth change only the crowded region? Put a directory of pointers in front of the buckets. A lookup uses g trailing hash bits to select one of 2^g pointers; g is the global depth. A bucket may be shared by pointers whose last d bits agree; d is that bucket’s local depth. Because g bits refine d bits, completed structures need d≤g. We use suffixes throughout this original trace; do not switch to leading bits halfway through.

Set g=2: labels 00,01,10,11. Bucket 01 has local depth d=2, capacity two, and hash values 1=001 and 5=101. Insert 9=1001. All three share suffix 01, so the current directory cannot separate them. Since d=g, first double the pointer table to g=3; then split only the full bucket using three bits.

Old labelBeforeAfter doubling and splitting
00target U00000→U00; 100→U00
01[1,5], d=2001→[1,9], d=3; 101→[5], d=3
10target U10010→U10; 110→U10
11target U11011→U11; 111→U11

The directory has eight pointers, but only one old bucket became two. U00,U10,U11 denote unchanged targets and need not be distinct. Doubling copies pointers, not every bucket’s data. Reinsert the affected entries by their new suffixes: 1 and 9 end in 001; 5 ends in 101. Check each new local depth is 3 and no larger than global depth 3.

When d<g before a split, the directory already distinguishes the extra bit. For g=3,d=1, four pointers share the bucket because the other g−d=2 bits have four combinations: 2^(g−d)=4. Splitting to d=2 divides them into two sets of two without doubling. This is extendible hashing: local growth can be handled by splitting just the affected bucket, with directory growth only when required.

Key takeaway

Doubling the directory enlarges only the pointer table. This step splits the full bucket; it does not copy every data bucket.

sections.title: Undo the split only when the distinctions are unnecessary
sections.html:
Continue the same state after inserting 9. Delete 9: bucket 001 becomes [1], while 101 holds [5]. Their local depths are both 3, their lower two bits agree (01), and together they fit capacity two. They are buddies: equal depth, identical suffix except for the highest bit used at that depth. Merge into [1,5] with d=2 and redirect both pointers. To shrink global depth from 3 to 2, every bucket must fit the shorter addressing scheme. In our trace all other buckets retained depths at most 2, so the directory can shrink to four pointers. A vacant slot alone would not justify shrinking.

Try a different state: g=3 and a bucket has d=1. How many pointers reach it? Split it once. How many pointers reach each result, and must the directory double?

Reasoned answer. Before: 2^(3−1)=4. After: each bucket has d=2 and 2^(3−2)=2 pointers. No doubling: the three-bit directory already provides the distinction. The local bucket split changes the targets of those four pointers, not all eight buckets.

Can repeated splitting separate three entries with exactly the same complete hash value when bucket capacity is two?

Reasoned answer. No. Every additional bit is still identical, so splitting cannot separate them. A practical design needs a collision/duplicate policy or another fallback; a toy “always split” loop can fail to terminate. Different keys with the same full hash still need key comparisons. Repeated copies of one key likewise cannot be separated by changing an ordinary key hash.

A correct trace therefore checks more than entry count: each key reaches the right suffix bucket; all pointers to a shared bucket are redirected consistently; completed local depth never exceeds global depth; merges preserve the required distinctions. Bucket and directory I/O, record fetches and writes remain real costs. Dynamic growth avoids many global rebuilds, but it does not make a hash lookup a guaranteed one-I/O query.

quiz.question: A bucket with local depth 2 and global depth 4 is split into buckets with local depth 3. Which statement is correct?
options: The directory does not need to double
quiz.explanation: Before the split the directory uses four bits. The split only needs three bits to distinguish the two new buckets, so the existing directory is already sufficient. The old bucket has 2^(4−2)=4 pointers; after redirection each new depth-three bucket has 2^(4−3)=2. Other buckets need not split.
